strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP evaluation problem: sensitivity to the choice of LLM judge. Its checklist framework is straightforward, requires no evaluator training, and makes score components directly inspectable.

The experimental coverage is substantial: 12 evaluator models, multiple model sizes, and SummEval, Topical-Chat, and QAGS. Reported human correlations generally improve, sometimes substantially for weaker evaluators, while variation in correlation across models decreases.

Human validation and analyses of augmentation, filtering, weighting, binarization, and inference budget provide useful supporting evidence. The code link, seed questions, prompt templates, and implementation details provide a foundation for reproduction.
weaknesses: The central agreement results require an implementation audit. After binarization, Table 14 reports G-Eval Large-model agreement of α=0.0090 but κ=0.5749. For the same complete binary ratings, nominal Krippendorff’s α and Fleiss’ κ should differ only by a small finite-sample correction. Similar discrepancies occur for already-binary groundedness in Table 25. The paper must explain the data layout, missing-value handling, and metric settings, and reconcile these results before the headline reliability improvement can support publication.

The unit of agreement is underspecified: individual checklist answers and aggregate text scores represent different evaluation targets. Thresholding G-Eval ratings in Appendix C.3 does not establish comparability if CheckEval agreement is measured over individual questions. Report question-level agreement separately from absolute agreement on normalized final scores. Likewise, reduced variance in modelwise human correlations does not directly establish reduced rating variance.

Several reporting inconsistencies undermine confidence in the empirical comparisons. For SEEval on SummEval, Table 1 gives Gemma2-27B Spearman correlation as 0.44, whereas Table 22 gives 0.4886; Gemma2-9B is 0.49 versus 0.4269. The human agreement study also reports approximately 10,000 answers per annotator for 100 summaries evaluated only on relevance, although Table 17 lists 26 relevance questions. These discrepancies need reconciliation against the underlying outputs.

Statistical uncertainty is insufficiently characterized. Main comparisons lack confidence intervals or paired significance tests, although improvements for stronger evaluators can be small and metric-dependent. The additional human correlation study contains only 20 summaries, and the 100-summary agreement study covers only relevance. Numerous checklist answers do not substitute for independent texts or establish broad human equivalence.

The experiments do not fully isolate the proposed mechanism. A Likert evaluator supplied with the same detailed subcriteria would help distinguish benefits of clearer criteria from benefits of binary responses. G-Eval’s probability-weighted scoring is not documented, and the three-sample experiment for one model on Topical-Chat does not establish a matched-compute comparison.

Some seed questions raise construct-validity concerns despite the emphasis on benchmark alignment. Table 27’s groundedness questions emphasize conversational flow and adding information without explicitly checking support from the supplied fact; Table 26’s relevance questions reward retaining source terminology, potentially penalizing valid paraphrases. An item-level audit and sensitivity analysis using alternative checklists would strengthen the claim that the framework faithfully measures the intended dimensions.
